source_refs.note: Topic 5.10, printed page 108. The printed heat of fusion of ice, 4.6 kJ per mol, is recorded as printed (the usual value is about 6.0).

blocks.text: Whenever matter undergoes a physical change it is accompanied by an energy change, and this change is the quantitative measure of the difference in strength of the intermolecular forces.

blocks.title: Molar heat of fusion
blocks.text: The amount of heat absorbed by one mole of a solid to melt it into the liquid at its melting point at 1 atmosphere is the molar heat of fusion, delta H f. For ice to water the printed value is 4.6 kJ per mol.

blocks.title: Molar heat of vaporization
blocks.text: The amount of heat absorbed by one mole of a liquid to convert it into one mole of vapour at its boiling point at 1 atmosphere is the molar heat of vaporization, delta H v. It depends on the strength of the intermolecular forces: one mole of water converted to vapour at 100 degrees C absorbs 40.6 kJ per mol.

Ammonia and hydrogen chloride need only 21.7 and 15.6 kJ per mol respectively to become vapour at their boiling points; the difference is due to the stronger intermolecular forces in water. The molar heats of fusion and vaporization affect the particles of matter by giving them enough energy to move away from one another, changing the state from solid to liquid and from liquid to gas; the particles gain more freedom to move and rotate in the liquid and gas phases. The heat of fusion of ice is important in the study of glaciers and ice sheets, including the polar ice caps.

blocks.prompt: Why is the molar heat of vaporization of water nearly three times that of hydrogen chloride, and why is the heat of fusion of ice important for polar ice caps?
blocks.explanation: Vaporizing a liquid means separating its molecules completely, so the heat needed measures the intermolecular forces. Water molecules are held by two hydrogen bonds each; HCl molecules only by weaker dipole-dipole and London forces, so far less heat frees them. Melting a mole of ice absorbs its heat of fusion without any rise in temperature, so the polar ice caps and glaciers can take in large amounts of heat while melting slowly, which governs how fast they shrink as the climate warms.

items: Molar heat of fusion: heat to melt one mole at the melting point (ice, printed 4.6 kJ per mol); molar heat of vaporization: heat to vaporize one mole at the boiling point (water 40.6, NH3 21.7, HCl 15.6 kJ per mol), larger for stronger forces.
The heat gives particles the energy to move apart and gain freedom; ice's heat of fusion matters for glaciers and polar ice caps.
